notes_context:
Memory items from past tasks:
- [rb-0001] Round monetary results with the project's round_money helper: Money values must be rounded via ledgerly.money.round_money (half-up to the cent), not Python's round() or bare Decimal.quantize(), which use banker's rounding.
  Before returning any computed money value, wrap it in the repository's round_money helper. Check the money module for existing conventions (ZERO, to_money, round_money) and mirror how sibling functions like line_total and invoice_total round their results.
- [rb-0006] Normalize money before range checks: Round/normalize monetary inputs via the project's money helper before comparing against zero so validation matches stored values.
  Call round_money(unit_price) first, then compare the rounded Decimal against ZERO. This ensures the stored value and the validation agree, and lets the helper raise its own errors (e.g. float_amount) for bad types.
- [rb-0008] Validate numeric fields defensively with bool exclusion: Checking period_days with isinstance(bool) exclusion plus int/positive checks guards against True/False and bad values before timedelta arithmetic.
  When validating an int field, remember bool is a subclass of int: reject it explicitly (`isinstance(x, bool) or not isinstance(x, int) or x <= 0`). Raise the project's domain error (BillingError) rather than ValueError/TypeError.
- [rb-0010] Check idempotency key before any validation: When a team convention requires idempotency, look up the audit log for the key first, before validating state or amounts, and return the original result.
  Scan audit.events(<event>) for a matching idempotency_key at the very top of the function and return the stored record unchanged. Only after that miss do amount/state checks; include idempotency_key in the audit entry you write.
- [rb-0012] Mirror sibling module patterns for new functions: Before implementing a stub, read sibling functions (payments.py) and shared helpers (money, clock, errors, audit) to copy rounding, validation order, and error codes.
  Reuse round_money/ZERO for all arithmetic, ensure_utc(at) for timestamps, and BillingError with the same code style (non_positive_amount, invalid_state) as existing functions. This keeps hidden tests and conventions satisfied without guessing.
- [rb-0002] Read existing sibling functions to infer conventions before implementing: The first attempt passed visible tests but was rejected for missing a rounding convention that sibling functions already followed.
  When adding a function to a module, inspect neighboring functions for patterns (rounding, type hints, zero-handling) and apply them consistently. Passing the visible test suite is not sufficient evidence that team conventions are met.

item.title: Match sibling module conventions before implementing
item.description: Reading payments.py, invoice.py, and money.py revealed the project's validation and rounding idioms, which the accepted implementation mirrored.
item.content: Before writing a new function, read 2-3 sibling modules that do similar work to learn the local conventions (error class, error codes, rounding helper, type coercion). Reusing those idioms makes the implementation fit and pass hidden tests.

item.title: Use Decimal(str(x)) for percent inputs, not float math
item.description: Converting rate_percent via Decimal(str(...)) avoids binary float artifacts and lets you validate finiteness and range cleanly.
item.content: When a numeric parameter is a rate/percent rather than money, coerce with Decimal(str(value)) inside try/except (InvalidOperation, ValueError), then check is_finite() and bounds. This handles ints, strings, and Decimals uniformly while rejecting NaN/inf.

item.title: Guard bools explicitly when validating numeric inputs
item.description: isinstance(rate_percent, bool) was checked first because bool is a subclass of int and would otherwise pass numeric validation.
item.content: In Python, True/False are ints, so numeric validators silently accept them. Add an explicit isinstance(x, bool) rejection before other type checks when a boolean should not be a valid amount or rate.
